content: Undoubtedly, there is a pressing need for more health professionals who possess new competencies and are motivated to address the evolving needs of society. Transforming the education of health professionals requires competent and dedicated leadership that prioritizes the health needs of populations and aligns with the objectives of the health service system. The World Health Organization (WHO) has initiated efforts to transform and scale up the education and training of health professionals, contributing to this challenging yet inspiring task. Initially, policy discussions on health workforce education focused on increasing educational capacity and production to address the shortage of health workers. This shortage was further exacerbated by migratory flows, predominantly from low-income to high-income countries. In response, the World Health Assembly (WHA) adopted the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel in 2010. Another critical issue was the inequitable geographical distribution of health workers, which led to the publication of WHO policy recommendations aimed at increasing access to health workers in remote and rural areas through improved retention strategies. The need to address deficiencies in the current approaches to health professional education in a systematic manner soon became evident. WHO, as a global normative and technical health agency, has taken responsibility for guiding countries in the transformative scaling up of health professional education. In 2009, WHO collaborated with the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) to strengthen the quality and capacity of nursing, midwifery, and medical education in Africa. This collaboration aimed to build a quantitatively stronger health workforce capable of meeting the health needs of individuals and communities. Scaling up education and training is a critical component of strategies to strengthen the health workforce. However, its effectiveness depends on complementary policies that retain graduates and provide them with conducive working conditions to utilize their knowledge and skills productively. WHO has broadened its focus to include a wider range of health professionals beyond doctors, midwives, and nurses, and has expanded its geographical scope beyond Africa, despite the high concentration of human resources for health crises in the region. The guidelines developed by WHO aim to serve various stakeholders, including government leaders, policymakers, educational institutions, students, health practitioners, educators, researchers, professional associations, regulatory bodies, health service managers, civil society, and development partners. These guidelines address key policy issues in five domains: education and training institutions, accreditation and regulation, governance and planning, financing and sustainability, and monitoring, implementation, and evaluation. However, they prioritize areas identified as critical by WHO and the Core Group, leaving some areas requiring further research. In many countries, these efforts must be undertaken amidst challenging economic circumstances. The link between education and health systems is vital, as education provides the essential resource of health professionals. There is a consensus that most countries face a shortage of healthcare providers, many of whom lack adequate training in terms of quality and relevance. New generations of health professionals must be equipped with appropriate competencies and the ability to lead change, adapting continuously to the evolving realities of health systems. Reforms in health professional education aim to develop competencies that are responsive to local needs while maintaining global connectivity. These reforms emphasize critical inquiry, effective use of information technologies, and a renewal of professionalism. The ultimate goal is a transformative and interdependent professional educational system that ensures equity in health. Achieving this goal requires mobilizing leadership within educational and health systems, increasing investments, developing robust quality control mechanisms, and strengthening global learning. Key questions for policymakers include how to recruit the right type of students, which competencies graduates should acquire, and what profile of educators and learning strategies are most appropriate. Additionally, identifying institutions best prepared to produce the desired quantity and quality of health professionals is crucial. Curricula must be adapted to produce professionals capable of continuous learning and adapting to new environments. Health professionals must also be able to navigate cultural variations, values, and attitudes toward different health problems. Interprofessional education (IPE) is increasingly recognized as essential for fostering collaboration across professional boundaries. Traditionally, health professional education has been conducted in silos, with each group developing its own competencies. However, today’s healthcare environment demands teamwork and collaborative practice models. IPE involves students from different professional programs learning together to enhance collaboration, teamwork, and ultimately patient-centered care. While initial research suggests positive outcomes, further evidence is needed to confirm its effectiveness in improving collaboration and patient care outcomes. Innovative teaching strategies, such as e-learning, offer significant potential for IPE. E-learning can be utilized in both high-income and resource-constrained settings, providing open access to education and enabling health professionals in remote areas to continue developing their competencies. However, not all competencies can be developed without interaction with trainers or peers, necessitating the use of blended or traditional strategies in some cases. Community-based learning approaches are also being developed to complement institutional and hospital-based training. The selection and recruitment of qualified educators and trainers are critical for scaling up and transforming health professional education. Faculty development is essential to ensure educators are well-prepared to fulfill their responsibilities. Incentives, such as access to faculty development, can help bridge the gap between teaching and clinical work, making the role of educators more attractive. Career structures, incentive systems, and reward mechanisms must be developed or improved to attract and retain educators, particularly those with competencies in primary care. Regulation and accreditation are essential components of strategies to improve healthcare system performance. Policymakers can use regulation to address workforce imbalances and other challenges, ensuring that health professionals are adequately trained to meet community needs. The state has a responsibility to protect citizens from poorly qualified providers and to facilitate the quality of health professional education. This includes ensuring sufficient numbers of health professionals are trained and that their training aligns with community needs.
